title: Hedwig (16 October)
hookLine: a duchess walks barefoot through the snow, carrying the shoes she was told to wear

cards: Winter in Silesia. A duchess is walking to church barefoot, on frozen ground, as she does to share a little of what the poor feel. Her confessor, worried, orders her to wear shoes.
She obeys. She carries them. That's the story people tell, half a joke and half a portrait: a woman who did what she was told, and still found a way to stand where the poor stood.

teach.h: GERMAN BY BIRTH, SILESIAN BY MARRIAGE.
teach.b: Hedwig was born into a noble family in Bavaria and married Henry, who became duke of Silesia, a land now mostly in Poland. German by birth and Silesian by marriage, she is honored today by both Germans and Poles.
In Polish, she's Jadwiga. She had wealth and power, and she spent a great deal of both on others.

teach.h: A CONVENT, HOSPITALS, BREAD FOR THE POOR.
teach.b: With her husband she founded a convent at Trzebnica for Cistercian nuns, and she supported hospitals and fed the poor, tradition says, sometimes serving them at her own table. Her life was not easy.
She outlived her husband and some of her children. Her son Henry was killed in battle defending the land against invaders.

teach.h: LAST YEARS IN THE CONVENT SHE FOUNDED.
teach.b: In her last years Hedwig lived at the convent she had founded, among the nuns, and she died there. What made her giving different? It wasn't only large gifts from a distance.
It was close: walking where the poor walked, eating with them, using her rank to open doors for them.
Paul has a line about that kind of giving, in the Douay-Rheims: "For God loveth a cheerful giver." The Greek word behind cheerful there is hilaros: glad. A glad heart, not a grim duty.
And it doesn't take a duchy.

In the same verse Paul says each one should give as he has decided in his heart, and a chapter earlier he says a gift is measured by what a person has, not by what he hasn't. Hedwig had a great deal and gave it gladly.
The same gladness fits a smaller purse.

how: Saint Hedwig is remembered on 16 October; she is honored in Poland and Germany, and Catholics in Silesia, especially at Trzebnica where she is buried, keep her feast with Mass and pilgrimage.

o: a German abbess who wrote hymns and music
a Hungarian queen who rode into battle
a duchess of Silesia who gave to the poor

s: Hedwig of Silesia is the same saint as Queen Jadwiga of Poland
they're two different women; Hedwig was a duchess of Silesia.
she was born in Bavaria and became duchess of Silesia by marriage.
the shoe story says she refused to obey her confessor
in the story she obeyed; she just carried the shoes.

games.q: you're Hedwig. your confessor orders you to stop walking barefoot in winter and wear shoes. what do you do?
o: ignore him and keep walking barefoot
put the shoes on and stop worrying
carry the shoes in your hands
games.why: the story people tell says she obeyed the order to have shoes, and carried them.

practice: Take a quiet inventory, not only your money but your time this week, a skill, a coat you don't wear, a meal you could share, and let one thing you could actually give rise to the top.
Notice whether the thought of giving it feels glad or grim. If you pray, offer it to God and ask for a cheerful heart; if you don't, simply let the glad part grow.

wordCard.voice: Hedwig. Jadwiga in Polish. A duchess of Silesia who founded a convent, fed the poor, walked where they walked, and gave gladly.

orig.note: the Greek word Paul uses for a cheerful giver in 2 Corinthians 9:7: glad, joyful.
